# Vana Saṁyutta (SN 9)

**ID:** SN 9
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Vana Saṁyutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Linked Discourses in the Woods
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/sn9

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vana Saṁyutta* (or *Vanasaṁyutta*, SN 9, PTS S I 197–205), titled the "Linked Discourses in the Woods", is the ninth division of the *Saṁyuttanikāya* [SuttaCentral; Tan 2004; Hazra 1994]. Unlike many larger *saṁyuttas*, it is not subdivided into subsidiary *vagga* sections and consists of fourteen short discourses accompanied by verses [SuttaCentral; Glass; Tan 2004]. The collection recounts the experiences of monks dwelling in forest solitude who exhibit negligence, slackness, or unwholesome thoughts; in each case, an observant forest deity (*devatā*) intervenes to admonish them, rousing spiritual urgency (*saṁvega*) and inspiring them back to diligent practice [SuttaCentral; Tan 2004; Hazra 1994; Williams 2005].

The *Vana Saṁyutta* is of exceptional text-critical significance for early Buddhist canonical history [Allon; Glass]. Complete sets of parallels to all fourteen discourses exist in both Chinese translations of the *Samyuktāgama* (T 99 and the partial translation T 100) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Glass; Salomon 2018], with individual Sanskrit parallels surviving in texts like the *Mahāvastu* [SuttaCentral]. In addition, an entire parallel group containing all fourteen sūtras is preserved in Gāndhārī on scroll 11 of the Senior manuscript collection, dating to around the first half of the second century CE [Allon; Glass; Salomon 2018; Bingenheimer]. Although the internal sequence of the fourteen discourses differs between the Gāndhārī, Chinese, and Pali recensions, the presence of this identical grouping across traditions indicates that the cluster was established well before the sectarian lines of transmission separated [Allon; Glass].

Text-reuse computations by DharmaNexus reflect extensive Pali-internal connections (1,355 matches with 82 texts), sharing shared verses and stock formulas with the *Brāhmaṇa Saṁyutta* (SN 7), *Devaputta Saṁyutta* (SN 2), several *nipātas* of the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (e.g., AN 3, AN 5, AN 6, AN 8), and commentarial corpora such as the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* and *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus cross-language alignments strongly mirror SuttaCentral's curated parallels in T 99 and T 100, while also detecting shared verse passages in Tibetan translations such as the *Mahākaruṇāpuṇḍarīkasūtra* [DharmaNexus].
